body.heading: Pick your day, not just your kite
paragraphs: Kites have been flown for well over two thousand years — the earliest were made in China, long before they became a toy. The physics hasn't changed since: a kite stays up when the wind pushes against its tilted surface hard enough to balance its weight.

What has changed is how easy it is to start. A classic diamond kite is the friendliest first kite there is, and it wants a steady breeze, roughly the kind that rustles leaves and moves small branches. If trees are standing still, wait for another day; if they are bending, the wind is too strong.

body.heading: Launch, fly, land
paragraphs: Find open ground away from roads, trees and power lines, and stand with your back to the wind. Hold the kite up with one hand and let out a little line with the other, then walk backwards slowly — or ask a friend to hold the kite and toss it gently upward as you pull. Short, steady tugs keep it climbing; reeling line in fast is what makes a kite dive.

When it is time to come down, walk toward the kite while winding the line in slowly. Never fly in a thunderstorm, and never fly near power lines. A kite that lands softly can be folded up and flown again next weekend — which is half the pleasure of it.

description: A steady breeze, a simple diamond kite and a little patience are all you need. Here's how to get it up, keep it up, and bring it down gently.
